title: Hypertension: Confirm, Risk-Stratify, Treat
bottomLine: Do not diagnose chronic hypertension from one casual office reading. Use validated standardized measurement and confirm with out-of-office readings when appropriate, then treat the patient's blood pressure in the context of overall cardiovascular risk, tolerability, comorbidity and goals.
recognize: Hypertension is often asymptomatic; end-organ symptoms suggest a different, urgent problem rather than 'symptomatic hypertension'.
Current Hypertension Canada primary-care guidance defines adult hypertension as BP at or above 130/80 mm Hg when measured with a validated device under optimal standardized conditions.
White-coat and masked hypertension are reasons to use home or ambulatory measurements.
differentiate: Chronic asymptomatic hypertension is not hypertensive emergency.

Secondary hypertension is more likely with abrupt onset, very young age, resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, episodic adrenergic symptoms, renal disease, sleep apnea clues or medication/substance causes.
assessment: Repeat BP using correct cuff size and standardized technique; assess both cardiovascular risk and orthostatic symptoms when relevant.
Review NSAIDs, stimulants, decongestants, oral contraceptives/estrogen, corticosteroids, licorice, alcohol and other contributors.
Assess smoking, diabetes, kidney disease, known cardiovascular disease, family history, diet, activity and sleep apnea risk.
workup: Confirm with out-of-office BP when feasible; obtain routine testing for cardiovascular risk and end-organ effects as indicated.
Use targeted secondary-cause testing only when history, examination or laboratory findings raise suspicion.
management: Recommend healthy lifestyle changes for all.
Hypertension Canada recommends pharmacotherapy at BP at or above 140/90 mm Hg and at systolic BP 130–139 mm Hg when cardiovascular risk is high.

For many patients needing medication, low-dose combination therapy using two complementary first-line classes is preferred; individualize for compelling indications, frailty, orthostasis, pregnancy potential and tolerance.
Aim for systolic BP below 130 mm Hg when treatment is well tolerated under the current primary-care guideline.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy and should be changed before conception when possible.
Check renal function and potassium after starting or titrating renin-angiotensin system blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists when used.
Avoid routine ACE inhibitor plus ARB combination therapy.
redFlags: BP elevation with acute neurologic deficit, encephalopathy, pulmonary edema, acute coronary syndrome, aortic syndrome, acute kidney injury, retinal emergency or pregnancy-related severe features
Severe symptomatic hypotension or recurrent falls after treatment
counselling: Teach correct home BP measurement and ask the patient to bring readings/device when useful.
Discuss sodium intake, physical activity, alcohol, smoking and weight in a non-stigmatizing way.
followUp: Reassess after initiation/titration soon enough to review BP, adverse effects and relevant laboratory monitoring.
Use home readings and orthostatic symptoms to avoid overtreatment.
examTrap: Treating a single nonstandardized high office reading as established chronic hypertension or sending an asymptomatic patient to the ED solely because the number is high.
oneLinePearl: Measure correctly, confirm outside the office, then treat risk—not one number.

title: Severe Blood Pressure: Emergency or Not?
bottomLine: The diagnosis of hypertensive emergency requires acute target-organ injury, not an arbitrary BP threshold alone. The NP's first job is to identify neurologic, cardiac, vascular, renal, retinal or pregnancy-related injury and escalate when present.
recognize: Concerning presentations include focal deficit, altered mental status, seizure, acute pulmonary edema, ischemic chest pain, tearing chest/back pain, acute kidney injury, visual loss or severe pregnancy-related symptoms.
Pain, anxiety, medication nonadherence and measurement error can cause markedly elevated BP without emergency organ injury.
differentiate: Hypertensive emergency: severe elevation plus acute target-organ damage.
Severe asymptomatic hypertension: no acute target-organ injury; generally requires confirmation, medication review and timely outpatient management rather than rapid IV reduction.
assessment: Repeat BP correctly in both arms when aortic pathology is possible; assess mental status, focal neurology, cardiopulmonary status, volume status and relevant funduscopic findings.
Ask about pregnancy/postpartum status, stimulant/cocaine use, missed medications, MAOI/sympathomimetic exposure and abrupt clonidine/beta-blocker withdrawal.
workup: Tailor ECG, troponin, creatinine/electrolytes, urinalysis, imaging, fundoscopy and pregnancy evaluation to suspected target-organ injury.
Do not order an identical broad panel for every asymptomatic high reading.
management: Emergency target-organ injury requires ED/hospital management with controlled BP reduction using the syndrome-specific approach.
Without acute injury, address reversible triggers, restart/intensify appropriate oral therapy and arrange close follow-up; avoid precipitous BP reduction.
medicationSafety: Rapid BP reduction can cause cerebral, coronary or renal hypoperfusion in chronically hypertensive patients.
Pregnancy/postpartum hypertension requires pregnancy-specific thresholds, medications and urgent obstetric pathways.
redFlags: Acute kidney injury with severe hypertension
Pregnancy/postpartum severe hypertension or preeclampsia features
counselling: Explain the difference between a high number and organ injury so the patient understands both the urgency when symptoms occur and the need for long-term control.
followUp: For severe asymptomatic hypertension managed outpatient, arrange prompt reassessment and confirm medication access/adherence.
examTrap: Choosing rapid normalization of BP in an asymptomatic patient instead of looking for target-organ injury first.
oneLinePearl: Treat the organ injury, not the panic generated by the number.

title: Dyslipidemia and ASCVD Prevention
bottomLine: Lipid treatment is risk-based. Separate secondary prevention and statin-indicated conditions from lower-risk primary prevention, then use shared decision-making about therapy, adherence and intensification.
recognize: Documented ASCVD is secondary prevention and generally warrants intensive lipid lowering unless contraindicated or inconsistent with goals of care.
Very high LDL-C or familial hypercholesterolemia, diabetes and CKD can create a statin-indicated condition even without prior ASCVD.
Nonfasting lipids are often acceptable; fasting testing is selectively useful, especially with substantial hypertriglyceridemia.
differentiate: Primary prevention decisions depend on global cardiovascular risk and risk modifiers, not LDL-C alone except at very high levels/familial hypercholesterolemia.
Over-the-counter fish-oil supplements are not equivalent to prescription evidence-based lipid therapies.
assessment: Assess smoking, BP, diabetes, kidney disease, premature family history, prior pregnancy-related cardiovascular risk conditions and established vascular disease.
Review secondary dyslipidemia causes and medications when the pattern is unexpected.
workup: Use a Canadian cardiovascular risk estimator when applicable; investigate severe hypertriglyceridemia or suspected familial dyslipidemia appropriately.
Measure liver enzymes or CK only when clinically indicated by therapy/risk rather than as indiscriminate recurring tests.
management: Health behaviour intervention remains foundational.
Use maximally tolerated statin therapy for secondary prevention; add nonstatin therapy when guideline thresholds remain above recommended levels despite tolerated statin treatment.
For primary prevention, match pharmacotherapy to absolute risk, statin-indicated conditions and patient preference.
medicationSafety: Check interactions with CYP-inhibiting drugs and assess unexplained muscle symptoms or hepatotoxicity when clinically indicated.
Pregnancy/planning pregnancy requires medication-specific review rather than automatic continuation of lipid-lowering therapy.
redFlags: Triglycerides high enough to raise pancreatitis concern
Possible familial hypercholesterolemia with premature ASCVD
New severe muscle pain/weakness with dark urine after statin initiation
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular risk and expected benefit rather than framing treatment around a single laboratory target.
Address medication cost and access if intensification is considered.
followUp: Repeat lipids after initiation/intensification to assess response and adherence, then at clinically appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Treating a low-risk patient's modest LDL elevation more aggressively than a high-risk patient with established ASCVD because the first laboratory number looks worse.
oneLinePearl: ASCVD risk determines urgency; the lipid panel refines the plan.

title: Chest Pain and Suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome
bottomLine: Suspected ACS is a time-sensitive diagnosis based on symptoms, ECG and serial cardiac biomarkers—not pain intensity. Stabilize and transfer urgently while simultaneously considering other lethal chest-pain diagnoses.
recognize: Pressure, heaviness, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, unexplained fatigue or epigastric discomfort can be ischemic presentations.
Women, older adults and people with diabetes may present without classic central chest pain.
A normal initial ECG or troponin does not automatically exclude early ACS.
differentiate: Cannot-miss alternatives include aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, esophageal rupture and pericarditis/tamponade.
Reproducible or pleuritic pain lowers but does not eliminate ACS probability.
assessment: Assess ABCs, vital signs, oxygenation when indicated, onset/character/radiation, exertional relationship, associated symptoms and cardiovascular risk.
Look for asymmetric pulses/BP, new murmur, heart failure, shock, DVT signs and alternate respiratory/GI clues.
workup: Obtain a 12-lead ECG urgently and use serial high-sensitivity troponin according to the local validated pathway.
Use chest imaging or additional testing based on alternative diagnoses; do not use a normal chest X-ray to rule out ACS.
management: Arrange emergency transfer/acute-care assessment when ACS is suspected.
Give evidence-based antiplatelet/anti-ischemic therapy according to the acute-care pathway after checking contraindications and competing diagnoses.
STEMI requires rapid reperfusion through the regional PCI/fibrinolysis system; do not delay transfer for outpatient investigations.
medicationSafety: Nitrates can worsen hypotension and are unsafe with recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure or certain preload-dependent states.
Avoid reflex oxygen in a normoxemic patient; use oxygen for hypoxemia/respiratory distress according to acute-care practice.
redFlags: ST elevation or dynamic ischemic ECG changes
counselling: Explain why emergency evaluation is needed even if symptoms improve because transient ischemia can precede infarction.
followUp: After ACS, ensure secondary prevention, cardiac rehabilitation, medication reconciliation and risk-factor management through a closed-loop transition.
examTrap: Sending a patient home because the first troponin or ECG is normal despite a concerning presentation.
oneLinePearl: ACS is a serial diagnosis—one normal early test is not the finish line.

title: Heart Failure With Reduced EF
bottomLine: In HFrEF, distinguish congestion from low-output instability, identify the precipitant, relieve volume overload, and build the four foundational disease-modifying medication classes as tolerated rather than maximizing one drug before starting the others.
recognize: Typical congestion clues include exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, edema, elevated JVP and rapid weight gain.
Low-output or shock features include hypotension, cool extremities, altered mentation, oliguria and rising lactate/creatinine.
Common decompensation triggers include ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled BP, kidney injury, medication nonadherence, NSAIDs and excess sodium/fluid.
differentiate: BNP/NT-proBNP supports but does not independently diagnose HF; values are influenced by age, renal function, obesity and AF.
Right-sided edema has many causes; use the whole clinical picture and echocardiography.
assessment: Assess volume status, perfusion, oxygenation, rhythm, BP, medication use, adherence and precipitating causes.
Ask about NSAIDs, high-sodium intake and medications that worsen HF.
workup: Use ECG, renal function/electrolytes, CBC and other cause-directed tests; obtain echocardiography to define EF and structure.
Evaluate ischemia, thyroid disease, iron deficiency and other contributors when indicated.
management: For chronic HFrEF, CCS foundational therapy consists of an ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB where appropriate), evidence-based beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor for most suitable patients.
Use loop diuretics to treat congestion; diuresis improves symptoms but is not a substitute for disease-modifying therapy.
Escalate decompensated HF with hypoxemia, hypotension, significant renal injury, ischemia or poor perfusion.
medicationSafety: Monitor renal function, potassium and BP during RAAS/ARNI/MRA titration.
SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative counselling and attention to genital infection and euglycemic ketoacidosis risk.
Do not start or aggressively titrate beta-blockade in cardiogenic shock or severe acute decompensation until stabilized.
redFlags: Severe hyperkalemia or acute kidney injury limiting therapy
counselling: Teach daily symptom/weight awareness, medication purpose, sodium moderation and when to seek care.
Address affordability and access because four-class therapy is ineffective if the patient cannot obtain it.
followUp: Reassess after medication changes for BP, heart rate, renal function, potassium, congestion and tolerance.
After hospitalization, early transition follow-up and medication reconciliation are high priority.
examTrap: Only increasing the loop diuretic while ignoring disease-modifying therapy or the precipitating cause.
oneLinePearl: Diuretics dry the patient out; foundational therapy changes the disease trajectory.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Failure Society HFrEF Guideline 2021

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Stability, Stroke, Symptoms
bottomLine: Approach AF in three decisions: Is the patient unstable? Does the patient need stroke prevention? Does rate or rhythm control best address symptoms and clinical context? Do not let rate control distract from anticoagulation assessment.
recognize: AF may cause palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, dizziness or no symptoms.
Confirm suspected AF with ECG or rhythm acquisition; an irregular pulse alone is a screen, not final documentation.
In Canada, CCS uses the CHADS-65 algorithm for antithrombotic decision-making in nonvalvular AF.
differentiate: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with shock, ischemia, pulmonary edema or severe altered perfusion requires urgent synchronized cardioversion pathway.
AF with manifest pre-excitation is dangerous: routine AV-nodal blocking rate-control drugs can accelerate conduction over the accessory pathway.
assessment: Assess hemodynamic stability, duration/onset, symptoms, stroke/TIA history, HF, hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease, bleeding factors and medication interactions.
Look for reversible contributors including infection, thyroid disease, alcohol, sleep apnea, ischemia, HF and stimulant exposure.
workup: Obtain 12-lead ECG and targeted electrolytes, CBC, renal function and TSH; echocardiography helps define structural disease.
Use ambulatory monitoring for intermittent symptoms when the diagnosis is not captured.
management: Unstable AF: urgent synchronized cardioversion through acute-care protocol.
Stable AF: choose rate or rhythm strategy based on symptoms, duration, comorbidity, age and patient preference; rhythm control is particularly relevant in recent-onset symptomatic AF.
Assess long-term antithrombotic therapy using the CCS CHADS-65 algorithm; anticoagulation decisions are separate from whether sinus rhythm is restored.
medicationSafety: Do not use acute AV-nodal blockers in AF with manifest pre-excitation.
Adjust DOAC choice/dose for renal function, interactions, age/weight criteria and indication; mechanical valves or moderate-severe mitral stenosis require a different anticoagulation approach.
Avoid routine long-term combination of OAC plus antiplatelet therapy in stable coronary disease without a specific indication because bleeding rises without clear ischemic benefit.
counselling: Discuss stroke risk, bleeding risk, adherence and what to do with missed anticoagulant doses.
Address modifiable drivers including BP, sleep apnea, obesity, inactivity, diabetes and alcohol misuse.
followUp: Reassess symptom control, heart rate, anticoagulant adherence/renal function and recurrence burden.
Confirm the patient understands when bleeding or stroke symptoms require emergency care.
examTrap: Selecting a rate-control medication and forgetting stroke prevention—or giving an AV-nodal blocker to pre-excited AF.
oneLinePearl: AF is not one problem: stabilize, prevent stroke, then control the rhythm/rate strategy.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society Atrial Fibrillation Guideline 2020
Thrombosis Canada Stroke Prevention in Atrial Fibrillation

title: Syncope: Find the Dangerous Cause
bottomLine: Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion. The exam priority is not naming every benign trigger; it is finding cardiac, hemorrhagic, thromboembolic or neurologic red flags that make discharge unsafe.
recognize: Vasovagal syncope often has a trigger and prodrome such as warmth, nausea, diaphoresis or visual dimming.
Orthostatic syncope relates to standing and may reflect volume depletion, autonomic dysfunction or medication effects.
Cardiac syncope is concerning when exertional, supine, abrupt without prodrome, associated with palpitations/chest pain, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease or family history of sudden death.
differentiate: Seizure is more likely with prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury or witnessed tonic-clonic activity; brief myoclonic movement can occur during syncope.
Presyncope can carry the same serious causes as complete syncope.
assessment: Clarify position, trigger, prodrome, duration, recovery, witness description, injury, exertion, palpitations/chest pain and medication/substance use.
Check orthostatic vitals when appropriate and perform focused cardiac and neurologic examination.
workup: Obtain ECG in unexplained syncope; additional laboratory/imaging tests should be driven by suspected cause.
Consider rhythm monitoring or echocardiography when arrhythmia/structural disease is plausible.
management: Emergency evaluation is required for high-risk cardiac features, major bleeding, PE features, severe anemia, persistent neurologic deficit or unstable vitals.
For clearly low-risk vasovagal/orthostatic syncope, treat triggers, hydration/medication contributors and provide recurrence precautions.
medicationSafety: Review antihypertensives, diuretics, vasodilators, QT-prolonging drugs, hypoglycemics and sedatives that can precipitate syncope/falls.
redFlags: Syncope during exertion or while supine
Chest pain, dyspnea or GI bleeding
counselling: Discuss injury prevention and activity/driving restrictions according to diagnosis and applicable provincial rules.
followUp: Unexplained or recurrent syncope needs a clear diagnostic follow-up plan; ensure high-risk patients are not lost to outpatient referral.
examTrap: Ordering head CT for every syncopal episode while missing the ECG and cardiac risk history.
oneLinePearl: In syncope, the history and ECG usually beat the shotgun panel.

title: DVT and Pulmonary Embolism
bottomLine: VTE diagnosis is probability-driven. Use a validated pre-test probability approach, then D-dimer and imaging strategically; suspected or confirmed PE becomes an emergency when hemodynamics or right-heart strain indicate high risk.
recognize: DVT: unilateral swelling, pain, tenderness or risk factors such as surgery, immobility, active cancer, prior VTE, estrogen exposure or pregnancy.
PE: unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope or hemoptysis; massive PE may present with shock or cardiac arrest.
A normal oxygen saturation does not rule out PE.
differentiate: Low pre-test probability plus all PERC criteria negative can avoid further PE testing in appropriately selected patients.
D-dimer is a rule-out test in selected low/intermediate-probability patients; it is not a diagnostic confirmation of VTE.
Pregnancy requires a pregnancy-appropriate diagnostic pathway rather than avoiding all imaging.
assessment: Assess hemodynamic stability first, then VTE risk factors, bleeding risk, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function and alternative diagnoses.
Look for signs of DVT, right-heart strain and competing causes of dyspnea/chest pain.
workup: Use validated pre-test probability to select D-dimer and compression ultrasound/CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q imaging.
After PE is diagnosed, risk-stratify using blood pressure/hemodynamics, RV findings, troponin/BNP and clinical/social factors.
management: High-risk PE with shock/hypotension requires emergency reperfusion-capable care and anticoagulation unless contraindicated.
When diagnostic testing will be substantially delayed and clinical probability is moderate/high, empiric anticoagulation may be appropriate if bleeding risk is acceptable.
Confirmed DVT/PE generally requires at least 3 months of anticoagulation; duration beyond that depends on provoking factors and recurrence/bleeding risk.
medicationSafety: DOACs are not the default in pregnancy/breastfeeding and may be inappropriate with significant renal/liver dysfunction, mechanical valves or high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome.
Before anticoagulation, check active bleeding, recent high-risk procedures, intracranial pathology and important drug interactions.
redFlags: Right-heart strain or positive cardiac biomarkers
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence, bleeding precautions and urgent symptoms of recurrent PE/DVT.
Discuss estrogen-containing therapy and transient provoking factors when relevant.
followUp: Reassess anticoagulation duration at the end of initial treatment, considering whether VTE was transiently provoked, persistent-risk or unprovoked.
Monitor renal function and bleeding risk according to chosen therapy.
examTrap: Ordering D-dimer in a clearly high-probability patient and using a positive result as if it confirms PE.
oneLinePearl: Probability chooses the test; hemodynamics choose the urgency.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada PE Diagnosis Clinical Guide 2025
Thrombosis Canada PE Treatment Clinical Guide 2025
Thrombosis Canada DVT Diagnosis/Treatment Clinical Guides 2025

title: Asthma: Control the Inflammation
bottomLine: Asthma is variable airflow obstruction driven by airway inflammation. Confirm the diagnosis objectively when feasible, assess control and future exacerbation risk separately, and ensure the treatment plan contains anti-inflammatory therapy rather than relying on bronchodilator relief alone.
recognize: Variable wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnea that change over time and with triggers support asthma.
Night symptoms, exercise limitation, frequent reliever use and prior severe exacerbations signal poor control or risk.
Normal examination between episodes does not exclude asthma.
differentiate: Consider COPD, inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, foreign body, dysfunctional breathing and medication-induced cough when the pattern is atypical.
Poor 'treatment response' may actually be incorrect inhaler technique, nonadherence, ongoing exposures or wrong diagnosis.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nighttime waking, activity limitation, exacerbations, oral steroid use, ED visits/intubation, smoking/vaping, occupational/allergic triggers and adherence.
Observe inhaler technique rather than asking only whether the patient knows how to use it.
workup: Demonstrate variable expiratory airflow limitation using spirometry/bronchodilator response or an appropriate alternative strategy when possible.
Use further testing when diagnosis remains uncertain rather than escalating indefinitely without confirmation.
management: Use an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing strategy appropriate to age and severity; current Canadian guidance for many adolescents/adults with mild asthma supports as-needed budesonide-formoterol as an anti-inflammatory reliever option.
Escalate controller therapy only after checking diagnosis, technique, adherence and triggers.
Acute severe exacerbation requires rapid bronchodilation, systemic corticosteroid therapy when indicated, oxygen for hypoxemia and escalation if poor response.
medicationSafety: Frequent SABA use without adequate anti-inflammatory therapy is a warning sign, not an acceptable long-term strategy.
Teach mouth rinsing after maintenance ICS where appropriate and spacer use for compatible devices.
Beta-blockers/NSAIDs can worsen asthma in susceptible patients.
redFlags: Poor response to initial bronchodilator therapy
counselling: Provide a written asthma action plan, trigger/smoking-vaping counselling and device-specific technique teaching.
In pregnancy, emphasize that uncontrolled asthma poses risk; do not stop effective controller therapy reflexively.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbation risk, technique and adherence after treatment changes and after an exacerbation.
examTrap: Adding another controller before checking inhaler technique/adherence—or treating mild asthma as SABA-only disease.
oneLinePearl: Asthma relief is not enough; treat the inflammation and the future risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Asthma Tools and Resources

title: COPD: Confirm Before You Label
bottomLine: COPD requires compatible exposure/symptoms plus persistent airflow obstruction confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry. Once confirmed, treatment is driven by symptom burden and exacerbation risk, alongside smoking cessation, vaccines, activity and inhaler technique.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum, recurrent lower respiratory infections and tobacco/occupational/biomass exposure support COPD.
Spirometry severity alone does not capture symptom burden or exacerbation risk.
differentiate: Asthma has greater variability and different inflammatory patterns; overlap can occur.
Heart failure, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, anemia and deconditioning may mimic COPD symptoms.
Do not label COPD from smoking history plus dyspnea without spirometric confirmation when the patient is stable.
assessment: Assess smoking/vaping, occupational exposures, dyspnea/activity, exacerbations/hospitalizations, oxygenation, weight, mood, inhaler technique and comorbid cardiovascular disease.
Ask about sputum changes and infectious symptoms during possible exacerbation.
workup: Confirm stable COPD with post-bronchodilator spirometry.
Use chest imaging, alpha-1 antitrypsin testing or other investigations when age, severity, family history or atypical features warrant.
management: Smoking cessation is the highest-value disease-modifying intervention for smokers.

Select long-acting bronchodilator therapy according to symptoms and exacerbation risk; add inhaled corticosteroid only for appropriate phenotypes/risk profiles rather than automatically for every patient.
Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and physical activity are core nonpharmacologic care.
During exacerbation, assess severity, bronchodilator needs, systemic steroids/antibiotics when indicated and whether acute-care escalation is required.
medicationSafety: Check inhaler technique and adherence before escalation.
ICS can increase pneumonia risk and should have a clear indication.
Avoid excessive oxygen in known chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure while still treating clinically important hypoxemia; titrate and reassess.
redFlags: Respiratory fatigue or altered mental status
counselling: Create an exacerbation action plan, reinforce smoking cessation supports, vaccines, exercise and correct inhaler use.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, exacerbations, technique, adherence and treatment adverse effects; repeat spirometry when it will change management rather than on an arbitrary schedule.
examTrap: Diagnosing COPD without post-bronchodilator spirometry or adding ICS simply because symptoms persist despite poor inhaler technique.
oneLinePearl: COPD is a spirometric diagnosis managed by symptoms plus exacerbation risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD Pharmacotherapy Guideline

title: Anaphylaxis: Epinephrine First
bottomLine: When anaphylaxis is suspected, give epinephrine promptly and activate emergency care. Antihistamines and inhaled bronchodilators are adjuncts; they do not replace epinephrine or treat shock/airway edema.
recognize: Rapid onset after an exposure with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise is anaphylaxis even without hives.
Multi-system involvement—skin/mucosa plus respiratory, GI or cardiovascular symptoms—supports the diagnosis.
Asthma can coexist with anaphylaxis; if uncertain during a likely allergic reaction, epinephrine is safer than delaying for an inhaler.
differentiate: Vasovagal reactions usually cause pallor/bradycardia and improve supine; anaphylaxis often causes tachycardia, flushing/urticaria, wheeze, swelling or hypotension.
Isolated hives without systemic features is not the same as anaphylaxis, but progression requires immediate reassessment.
assessment: Assess airway swelling/voice, work of breathing/wheeze, blood pressure/perfusion, GI symptoms and skin/mucosal findings.
Identify the likely trigger but do not delay treatment to prove it.
workup: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis; laboratory testing should never delay epinephrine.
Serum tryptase may support later evaluation in selected cases but a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.
management: Give intramuscular epinephrine promptly using the age/weight-appropriate device/dose and activate EMS/acute-care transfer.
Repeat epinephrine if symptoms are not improving according to emergency guidance; position safely, provide oxygen/IV fluids and airway support as needed.
Use inhaled bronchodilator for persistent bronchospasm and antihistamine for cutaneous symptoms only after epinephrine.
medicationSafety: There is no absolute contraindication to epinephrine when treating true anaphylaxis.
Do not substitute antihistamines or corticosteroids for epinephrine.
counselling: Before discharge after acute-care assessment, ensure access to appropriate epinephrine device(s), technique teaching, trigger avoidance guidance and allergy referral when indicated.
followUp: Patients treated with epinephrine require emergency medical assessment/observation; future plans should include an anaphylaxis action plan and device replacement before expiry.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine first because the patient has hives while airway or circulatory symptoms are evolving.
oneLinePearl: Anaphylaxis is epinephrine first—everything else is secondary.
